headline: Roosters win a thriller NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Knights, gold prices surge to record highs, and Iran's drone war in the Middle East escalates — a big Friday on all fronts.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS bounced +1.54% today but remains deeply underwater — down 61% on your total investment. Lithium prices globally are under severe pressure again, with market reports flagging another wave of price declines hitting ASX lithium stocks hard. Today's small pop is welcome but doesn't change the tough backdrop.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI had a solid session, up 1.34% today, riding the broader AI theme and strong overnight gains on the NASDAQ last session. The ETF holds AI infrastructure and tech names that benefited from positive sentiment around data centre demand and AI growth.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG rose 0.67% today, tracking the ASX 200's solid session (up 0.8%) and reflecting last night's strong US markets. As a diversified high-growth fund, it captures gains across both Australian and international equities.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS closed up 0.65% today on the ASX, reflecting last night's big NASDAQ rally (+1.9%) and S&P 500 gains (+1.43%). The US market had a strong session driven by tech, which flows directly into this fund.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO edged up 0.45% last night in a generally positive NASDAQ session. GTA 6 buzz continues in gaming circles, and separately Rockstar Games workers voted against unionising — removing a potential cost/disruption risk for the business.

movers.name: DHHF (BetaShares Diversified All Growth)
movers.note: DHHF gained 0.48% today, tracking broad market strength. As a diversified all-growth ETF, it benefits when both the ASX and global equities have positive sessions — which both did today.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: GOOG crept up 0.26% last night but remains about 15% below where it was a year ago. Despite Google Cloud revenue more than doubling, analysts note the market is pricing in AI competition concerns and antitrust risk — weighing on the share price despite strong underlying business performance.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: MSFT nudged up 0.3% last night but is still down roughly 7.6% since its last earnings report. The market has been cautious on Microsoft's near-term AI spending versus returns, though the long-term cloud and AI thesis remains well intact.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE barely moved today, up just 0.07%. Emerging markets continue to face headwinds from geopolitical uncertainty (particularly in the Middle East) and a stronger US dollar environment — the fund is flat to slightly negative on your overall investment.

watch_today.title: Pilbara Minerals (PLS.AX) — lithium price crash is the real story
watch_today.detail: PLS bounced +1.54% today but you're still down 61% on your investment. Market reports today flagged lithium prices are crashing again, hammering ASX lithium stocks. The core problem hasn't changed: global lithium oversupply. For a long-term holder, the question is whether you believe in a lithium recovery over the next 3-5 years. If yes, sit tight. If your conviction has changed, it's worth a rethink — but selling now locks in a large loss.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — good day, still underwater overall
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF had a solid session today (+1.34%), riding NASDAQ momentum. You're still down about 20% on your total investment though. The long-term AI infrastructure story remains compelling — data centre demand, power requirements, and AI compute are all growing. Unless your view on AI's future has changed, this is a hold and keep watching.

watch_today.title: GOOG — down 15% over the past year despite record Cloud growth
watch_today.detail: Alphabet is in an interesting spot: Google Cloud revenue more than doubled, yet the stock is down ~15% year-on-year. The market is nervous about AI competition (OpenAI, Microsoft) and ongoing antitrust pressure. At current prices, some analysts are calling it undervalued given the Cloud trajectory. For a long-term holder, the investment thesis is still intact — Google remains a dominant business. No reason to sell; worth watching if the AI competition narrative shifts.

watch_today.title: Gold surges 3.57% — a signal worth watching
watch_today.detail: Gold hit $3,662 USD per ounce last night, up a massive 3.57% in a single session. That kind of spike usually signals investors are nervous about something — geopolitical risk (the Iran/Kuwait situation is escalating), inflation fears, or uncertainty about central banks. Gold is a 'fear trade'. You don't hold gold directly, but it's worth noting as a backdrop for your broader portfolio positioning.

watch_today.title: RBA rate debate heating up — inflation jump complicates things
watch_today.detail: There's a noisy debate in Australian financial media today: some economists are demanding the RBA cut rates ASAP, while others warn a fresh inflation jump means the RBA might actually need to hike again. This directly affects mortgage holders, spending power, and ASX valuations. Watch next week for any RBA commentary — if rate hike talk gets louder, it could weigh on VDHG and DHHF (which hold Australian equities).

watch_today.title: MSFT & TTWO — solid long-term holdings, no action needed
watch_today.detail: Both Microsoft and Take-Two had quiet but positive sessions last night. MSFT is still digesting post-earnings softness (down ~7.6% since last report) but its AI and cloud business is structurally strong. TTWO continues to benefit from GTA 6 anticipation. Both are long-term holds — no catalysts today that change the picture.

world.summary: The Middle East conflict continues to escalate with Iran now accused of a deadly drone attack in Kuwait, drawing European calls for tougher pressure on Tehran. Gold is spiking on global fear. The UN is warning of worsening hunger across the region.

stories.title: Iran accused of deadly drone attack in Kuwait — EU calls for tougher action on Tehran
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has been accused of launching drone strikes inside Kuwait, killing at least two Italian Rheinmetall engineers working there — a significant escalation that takes the conflict beyond Israel and Gaza into a Gulf state that has traditionally stayed out of the fighting. The EU is now calling for stepped-up pressure on Tehran in response. Italy is separately being lined up to lead a European peacekeeping mission in Lebanon. This is the conflict spreading geographically, which raises the stakes for global oil supply and regional stability.

stories.title: China's role in the Iran war: peacemaker or quietly profiting?
stories.why_it_matters: The Lowy Institute has published an analysis asking whether China is acting as a genuine peace broker in the Middle East conflict — or whether it's quietly benefiting by buying cheap sanctioned Iranian oil and selling weapons-capable tech. This matters for Australia because if China is seen as enabling Iran, it complicates the geopolitical picture for Western allies and could affect Australia-China trade relations. It also influences how the conflict ends, since China has real leverage over Iran that it may or may not choose to use.

stories.title: UN warns hunger will deepen across the Middle East
stories.why_it_matters: The United Nations is warning that food insecurity will worsen significantly across the Middle East as the conflict drags on. Supply chains for food and fuel across the region are being disrupted by fighting, blockades, and displacement. Beyond the immediate human toll, rising hunger in a volatile region historically fuels further instability and refugee flows — which eventually become political issues for countries like Australia as well.

stories.title: Tanker shipping rates set for two-year decline — regardless of Middle East conflict
stories.why_it_matters: Shipping industry body BIMCO is forecasting that tanker freight rates will fall for the next two years — even if the Middle East conflict continues. This is because a wave of new ships ordered during the COVID supply crunch are now entering service, adding capacity faster than demand is growing. Lower shipping costs are generally good for global trade and inflation, but it's a headwind for shipping companies and signals the global economy isn't roaring ahead.

stories.title: Gold price surges 3.57% to $3,662/oz — investors seeking safety
stories.why_it_matters: Gold had one of its biggest single-session jumps in recent memory overnight, rising 3.57% to $3,662 USD per ounce. When gold spikes this sharply it usually means investors are rushing to safe-haven assets — typically because of geopolitical fear, inflation worries, or distrust of central banks. The Iran escalation into Kuwait is likely a key driver. For everyday Australians, rising gold prices can lift Australian mining stocks and signal broader economic uncertainty ahead.

markets.summary: Last night's US session was strong — the NASDAQ jumped nearly 2% and the S&P 500 gained 1.43%, driven by tech. The ASX followed suit today, adding 0.8%. Gold surged over 3.5% on geopolitical fear. Oil dipped slightly. The Aussie dollar is holding steady around 66.5 US cents.

indicators.note: Solid session today, up 0.8%, riding the coattails of last night's strong US markets.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Strong session last night — up 1.43%, led by tech and growth stocks.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: NASDAQ was the standout last night, rising 1.9% — AI and tech names led the charge.

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Massive spike — up 3.57% as investors sought safety amid escalating Middle East tensions.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil dipped 1.16% last night despite Middle East tensions — tanker oversupply and demand concerns weighing.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar edged up slightly, holding around 66.5 US cents.

politics.summary: Australia is missing its 2035 climate targets, the gas reservation scheme has passed parliament, the RBA faces mounting pressure over rates and inflation, and there's controversy over new powers given to Defence Minister Marles.

stories.title: Australia on track to completely miss its 2035 emissions target
stories.why_it_matters: New projections show Australia will fall well short of its 2035 climate emissions target without major new policy action — this is a significant political problem for the Albanese government, which has staked credibility on climate action. It also matters economically: falling short of targets could affect trade relationships with the EU (which is introducing carbon border taxes) and Australia's ability to attract green investment. Critics from both left (not enough action) and right (COP31 'failure') are piling on.

stories.title: Gas reservation scheme passes parliament
stories.why_it_matters: The federal government has passed a gas reservation scheme through parliament, meaning gas companies will now be required to set aside a portion of their production for the domestic Australian market rather than exporting it all. The goal is to keep gas supply and prices lower for Australian households and businesses. Whether it works is debated — The Conversation notes the policy relies on market mechanisms that may not deliver lower prices at the household level. Gas and energy companies may face lower export revenue as a result.

stories.title: RBA under fire — should it cut or hike rates?
stories.why_it_matters: Australian inflation has jumped again, sparking a fierce debate: some economists and commentators say the RBA (Reserve Bank) has gone too far with high rates and must cut immediately to relieve mortgage stress, while others warn the inflation data means the RBA may need to raise rates again. This directly affects every Australian with a mortgage — higher rates mean bigger repayments. It also matters for the share market, as higher rates typically push equity valuations down. The RBA's next move is now a live question.

stories.title: Defence Minister Marles granted power to override laws to assist the US
stories.why_it_matters: The Saturday Paper reports that Defence Minister Richard Marles has been quietly granted new powers to override Australian laws in order to assist the United States military — with critics calling it a 'flat-out lie' about the nature of the AUKUS alliance commitments. This raises significant sovereignty questions: how much autonomy does Australia retain over its own legal framework when US military interests are involved? It's likely to become a major political controversy as more details emerge.

stories.title: Victoria election guide — parties and their key promises
stories.why_it_matters: With a Victorian state election on the horizon, The Guardian has published a plain-English guide to what each party is promising — covering Labor, the Coalition, Greens, and minor parties. Key battlegrounds include housing affordability, energy costs, public transport, and health. Worth a read if you have family or interests in Victoria, as state policies on planning and energy can have real flow-on effects for property values and cost of living.

ai.summary: It's Black Friday in the AI world too — Google and Adobe are cutting subscription prices while OpenAI and Anthropic are holding firm. OpenAI scores a win on robotics benchmarks, and AI regulation remains stuck in the US Congress.

stories.title: Black Friday AI deals: Google cuts prices, OpenAI and Anthropic don't budge
stories.why_it_matters: Google (Gemini) and Adobe are offering genuine Black Friday discounts on their AI subscriptions this week, while OpenAI (ChatGPT) and Anthropic (Claude) are keeping their prices unchanged — signalling different competitive strategies. Google appears willing to discount to win users, while OpenAI is betting its product is premium enough to hold full price. For everyday users, there are deals worth grabbing: one deal bundles ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and other AI tools for a one-time $65 payment. Good timing to lock in an AI tool if you've been on the fence.

stories.title: OpenAI beats Google and Anthropic on humanoid robot benchmark
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI has topped a new benchmark test for AI systems designed to control humanoid robots — beating out Google and Anthropic. This matters because the race to build AI that can operate physical robots (in factories, warehouses, homes) is heating up fast. OpenAI is showing it's not just a chatbot company — it's competing at the frontier of embodied AI, which is where the next wave of automation is likely to come from. This is relevant to your GXAI.AX holding, which invests in AI infrastructure companies.

stories.title: AI still trails human lawyers — new Prysm benchmark finds
stories.why_it_matters: A new benchmark called Prysm has tested AI systems against human lawyers on complex legal reasoning tasks — and found AI still falls meaningfully short. This is a useful reality check amid all the hype: AI is excellent at research, drafting, and summarising, but it still makes mistakes that an experienced lawyer wouldn't. For anyone worried about AI replacing their job or profession, this suggests the transition will be slower and more partial than the most dramatic predictions.

stories.title: US Congress deadlocked on AI regulation — bipartisan desire, no agreement
stories.why_it_matters: The New York Times reports that despite both Democrats and Republicans agreeing that AI needs some form of regulation, Congress can't agree on what that should look like — leaving the US without federal AI rules. The main obstacles are disagreements over whether to prioritise innovation or safety, and which agencies should be in charge. Without clear rules, big tech companies (including Google and Microsoft, which you hold) face an uncertain regulatory environment — but in the short term, less regulation generally means more freedom to move fast.

sport.summary: The Roosters have won the NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Knights in a thriller at Accor Stadium. Sam Walker is heading to PNG in 2028. Jannik Sinner is out of the Australian Open after knee surgery. AFL trade season continues with some big moves.

stories.title: Roosters win the NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Knights
stories.why_it_matters: In one of the great Grand Finals, the Sydney Roosters have beaten the Newcastle Knights 19-18 at Accor Stadium. One point the difference — it doesn't get tighter than that. A massive result for the Roosters who claim another premiership, and heartbreak for the Knights who came agonisingly close.

stories.title: Sam Walker signs with PNG Chiefs for 2028 NRL season
stories.why_it_matters: Sydney Roosters halfback Sam Walker — the 2026 premiership-winning halfback — has signed with the PNG Chiefs for the 2028 NRL season. The PNG Chiefs, NRL's expansion team, have been on a massive spending spree signing marquee names. Walker joins a growing list of big signings as PNG builds toward becoming a genuine NRL force. This is a huge cultural moment for Papua New Guinea rugby league.

stories.title: Jannik Sinner ruled out of the Australian Open after knee surgery
stories.why_it_matters: World No. 1 Jannik Sinner has been ruled out of the 2027 Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery. Sinner is a two-time Australian Open champion, so his absence is a massive blow for the tournament's drawcard appeal. It opens the door for Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, and others to claim the title without having to beat the world's best player.

stories.title: AFL off-season: Collingwood star departs, Western Bulldogs sign VFL gun
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL trade and free agency period continues to generate headlines. A Collingwood heavyweight has left the club reportedly due to 'tension' with the premiership coach — a sign of some internal friction at the premiers. Separately, the Western Bulldogs have signed a 25-year-old VFL standout, while an interstate rival has poached a Hawthorn father-son prospect. The off-season shape-up is well underway across the competition.
